answer:
Let the two readings be  
\[
x_1=10.0\pm 0.4,\qquad x_2=11.0\pm 0.3,
\]
so the equally weighted mean is
\[
\bar x=\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}=10.5.
\]

### 1. Worst-case bounded errors
The error in the mean is
\[
\delta \bar x=\frac{\delta x_1+\delta x_2}{2}.
\]
Worst case adds magnitudes:
\[
|\delta \bar x|_{\max}=\frac{0.4+0.3}{2}=0.35.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\bar x=10.5\pm 0.35\quad\text{(worst-case bound)}}.
\]
Equivalently, the range is \(10.15\) to \(10.85\).

### 2. Independent zero-mean errors with standard deviations \(0.4\) and \(0.3\)
For independent errors,
\[
\sigma_{\bar x}=\frac12\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}
=\frac12\sqrt{0.4^2+0.3^2}
=\frac12\sqrt{0.16+0.09}
=0.25.
\]
So the one-standard-deviation uncertainty is
\[
\boxed{\bar x=10.5\pm 0.25\quad(1\sigma)}.
\]

### Perfectly shared proportional fluctuations
Yes, that would change the second calculation, because the errors would no longer be independent. In general,
\[
\sigma_{\bar x}^2
=\frac14\left(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2+2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2\right).
\]
For perfectly positively correlated errors, \(\rho=1\),
\[
\sigma_{\bar x}=\frac{0.4+0.3}{2}=0.35,
\]
rather than \(0.25\).

If the shared fluctuation is a common relative fluctuation \(f\), then to first order the errors are proportional to the readings:
\[
\delta x_1\approx 10f,\qquad \delta x_2\approx 11f,
\]
and
\[
\sigma_{\bar x}=10.5\,\sigma_f.
\]
The quoted fractional uncertainties are not equal, \(0.4/10=0.04\) and \(0.3/11\approx0.0273\), so the two given uncertainties cannot both come solely from one common proportional fluctuation. A mix of common and independent components would require the covariance term above.

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Worst-case: }10.5\pm0.35,\\
&\text{Independent zero-mean: }10.5\pm0.25\ (1\sigma),\\
&\text{Perfectly correlated/shared fluctuations: use covariance; for }\rho=1,\ \sigma_{\bar x}=0.35.
\end{aligned}}
\]
